extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, jurists, legislators, and general readers interested in theories of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts John Locke's normative criteria for the origin, limits, and ends of civil government: definitions of political power, the state of nature/war, property, punishment, consent, and slavery. Useful for evaluating whether a government or law meets Locke's standards of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Political Power
rubrics_metrics.description: "POLITICAL POWER... to be a RIGHT of making laws with penalties of death, and consequently all less penalties, for the regulating and preserving of property, and of employing the force of the community, in the execution of such laws, and in the defence of the commonwealth from foreign injury; and all this only for the public good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes political power from paternal, marital, master/servant, or lord/slave powers; emphasizes that legitimate political power is law-making with enforceable penalties, exercised for the public good only.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of Nature (Freedom and Equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A state of perfect freedom to order their actions, and dispose of their possessions and persons, as they think fit, within the bounds of the law of nature... A state also of equality, wherein all the power and jurisdiction is reciprocal, no one having more than another."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty in the state of nature is not licence; actions remain bounded by the law of nature. The state of nature ends only by mutual consent to form a political society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Nature and Reason as Its Law
rubrics_metrics.description: "The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges every one: and reason, which is that law, teaches all mankind... that no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason provides binding moral standards for conduct; these standards are intelligible and can be executed by individuals in the absence of civil society. Municipal laws are right only insofar as they conform to this law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and Duty to Punish (Execution of the Law of Nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The execution of the law of nature is, in that state, put into every man’s hands, whereby every one has a right to punish the transgressors of that law to such a degree, as may hinder its violation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every person may proportionately punish offenders for reparation and restraint; punishment must be governed by calm reason and conscience and proportionate to the transgression to prevent repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Limits of the State of War
rubrics_metrics.description: "THE state of war is a state of enmity and destruction: and therefore declaring by word or action... a sedate settled design upon another man’s life, puts him in a state of war with him..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of war arises from declared designs of force; it justifies treating aggressors as enemies (including killing in self-defence). The absence of a common judge turns disputes into a state of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of Self-Preservation and Prioritizing Innocent Safety
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every one, as he is bound to preserve himself... when his own preservation comes not in competition, ought he, as much as he can, to preserve the rest of mankind..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-preservation is fundamental; when not in competition, individuals should preserve others. When all cannot be preserved, the safety of the innocent is to be preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of Property by Labour
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatsoever then he removes out of the state that nature hath provided, and left it in, he hath mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and thereby makes it his property."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing one's labour with common resources appropriates them, so long as there remains 'enough, and as good' for others; examples include gathering acorns, drawing water into a pitcher, digging ore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso on Appropriation ('Enough and as Good' Condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke's proviso that appropriation is valid 'at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation by labour is limited: one may not appropriate in a way that leaves others worse off by depriving them of comparable resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and Formation of Political Society
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not every compact that puts an end to the state of nature between men, but only this one of agreeing together mutually to enter into one community, and make one body politic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil government arises from the mutual consent of individuals to form a commonwealth; other bargains do not end the state of nature. Legitimate legislative authority derives from this consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom under Government (Limit on Arbitrary Power)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This freedom from absolute, arbitrary power, is so necessary to, and closely joined with a man’s preservation, that he cannot part with it, but by what forfeits his preservation and life together..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals cannot legitimately transfer absolute arbitrary power over their lives; liberty under government means subjection only to laws established by the legislature by consent, not to the caprice of any man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery Defined and Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is the perfect condition of slavery, which is nothing else, but the state of war continued, between a lawful conqueror and a captive..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slavery is the continuation of a state of war after conquest; voluntary sale typically creates service/drudgery, not absolute slavery. One cannot lawfully enslave oneself (cannot transfer power over one's life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Public Punishment and Private Reparation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The magistrate... can often... remit the punishment of criminal offences by his own authority, but yet cannot remit the satisfaction due to any private man for the damage he has received."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public authorities may forgive or commute criminal penalties for public reasons, but they cannot extinguish an injured private person's right to reparation; injured parties retain a separate right to seek satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Legitimacy from Historical Succession Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke's refutation that current rulers derive authority from Adam: "it is impossible that the rulers now on earth should make any benefit, or derive any the least shadow of authority from that... Adam’s private dominion..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy cannot rest on claimed descent from a mythical or unprovable original dominion; governments must be grounded in more immediate origins (consent, compact, or conquest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perverting Justice Reinstates a State of War
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 'the remedy is denied by a manifest perverting of justice, and a barefaced wresting of the laws to protect or indemnify the violence or injuries of some men', Locke contends that 'there it is hard to imagine any thing but a state of war.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government that systematically perverts law to protect injustice effectively places its subjects back into a state of war, justifying resistance or appeal beyond earthly courts.
